canonical_name: Chebyshev's probability inequality (exact source formulation and duplicate-target allocation open)
literal_source_claim_zh: 随机变量偏离期望的概率上界
literal_source_claim_en: An upper bound on the probability that a random variable deviates from its expectation.
statement_blocker: The catalog fixes a probability-deviation theorem family but provides no formula, probability-space encoding, random-variable codomain, measurability or moment assumptions, event strictness, threshold domain, variance codomain, coercion policy, or boundary cases. The inspected 1867 sum theorem calls its quantities arbitrary while its proof uses product joint weights and thus unstated mutual independence; it also omits the positive/nonzero domain of alpha and uses a strict inside-event bound requiring a checked complement transport. The catalog also gives THM-M-0992 the same title, attribution, year, and probability-tail gloss, while that target's dossier makes an unsupported conflicting claim that THM-M-0282 is the deterministic sum inequality. An immutable pinpoint source statement, original/translation and priority audit, independent review, and a master-owned duplicate-ID allocation decision are required before selecting an exact proposition.
domain_and_universes: Open: an approved source and duplicate-ID decision must fix the probability sample-space universe and measurable structure, probability-measure encoding, random-variable codomain, moment and measurability package, threshold type, and every Lean typeclass and coercion. Arbitrary finite measures are a generalized formal candidate, not the source semantics.
conclusion: Prospective family only: the probability of a two-sided deviation of a random variable from its expectation is bounded above using its variance or second moment. The exact event, threshold, codomain, and formula are open.
degenerate_case_status: No case is excluded before a proposition is selected; the statement phase must resolve zero and negative thresholds, constant and zero-variance variables, empty or null spaces, infinite or nonexistent moments, closed versus strict events, and real versus extended variance.
